script.opening: “Hi. Thanks for doing it on video. I need the morning-after pill — I know it’s late — and an STI test. Something happened at work and I just want it sorted.”

facts.text: “Saturday, about eleven at night.” (Now Monday afternoon — about 40 hours.) Period started 13 days ago; cycle regular, 28 days.

facts.topic: Work (if asked what you mean by work)
facts.text: Pause, then: “I’m an escort. Independent — I work from a flat I rent. I’m also a student nurse.” Watch the doctor’s reaction.
“He took the condom off halfway. I didn’t agree to that. When I told him to stop he slapped me and grabbed my arm. Then he left.” Ejaculated inside. Vaginal only.

Bruise on left upper arm (can show on camera), sore cheek. No loss of consciousness, no headache now, no vomiting, no vision problems. If asked about the neck: “No, nothing round my neck.” No genital bleeding; a bit sore.
“A regular-ish. I don’t know his HIV status. I don’t think he’s from a high-risk group but I don’t know.” You have his phone number.

No contraception other than condoms. Stopped the pill in 2024 because of mood. No regular medicines. No liver problems, no epilepsy medicines. Hepatitis B: “I had one injection at uni — not sure about the rest.”
No one takes your money or controls you. You work alone. “I’m a bit scared to go back to the flat.”
“Shaky. Not sleeping. I keep replaying it.” No thoughts of harming yourself. Drinking a bit more wine since.
“I don’t want the police. They’ll judge me.”

facts.topic: Your fear (only if asked what worries you most, or about confidentiality)
facts.text: “Will this go on my record? If my university finds out I do sex work, I’ll be kicked off the course.”

Be matter-of-fact at first, testing whether the doctor judges you. If the doctor reacts awkwardly or moralises, keep answers short and do not mention the slap. If the doctor is calm and non-judgemental, describe what happened. When the doctor explains confidentiality clearly, relax visibly. Agree to go to the sexual health clinic today if the doctor explains the time limit for PEP and the IUD. You may want to think about the SARC.

ice.ideas: “I just need the morning-after pill and a test.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — that her GP record or the GP will tell her university about her sex work and end her nursing career; also fear of HIV and of being judged by police.
ice.expectations: A pill today and STI tests; no fuss.

checkpoints.text: Establishes the timeline (about 40 hours), cycle day 13, contraceptive history and interacting medicines
Asks non-judgementally about the incident and recognises non-consensual condom removal and assault; screens injuries including head injury and strangulation
Assesses safety, third-party control or coercion, mood, alcohol and support

Offers emergency contraception correctly: copper IUD most effective (up to 5 days), and oral ulipristal today in case the IUD is delayed; advises waiting 5 days before starting hormonal contraception after ulipristal
Arranges same-day sexual health clinic or SARC assessment for HIV PEP (within 72 hours), hepatitis B vaccination and STI tests, with repeat testing at window periods
Explains SARC options (forensic examination within days, self-referral without police), police reporting as her choice, and anonymous reporting schemes for sex workers
Explains confidentiality accurately: no disclosure to her university; limits only for serious risk of harm; discusses record wording
Maintains a calm, non-judgemental, trauma-informed tone, validates that what happened was not her fault, and agrees a shared plan she can carry out today

worked.txt: “Thanks for telling me. Can you tell me as much as you’re comfortable with about what happened?”
“Removing a condom without your agreement isn’t a contraception accident — it can be a serious sexual offence, and hitting you is assault. None of this is your fault.”

“There are two clocks running. HIV prevention medicine has to start within 72 hours, so we have about a day and a half. And the coil, which is the most effective emergency contraception, can go in up to five days.”
“I’ll prescribe ulipristal today so you’re covered if the coil can’t be fitted straight away. If you take it, wait five days before starting any pill.”

“What you tell me stays between you and the health team. I won’t tell your university — that’s not my role and I wouldn’t. I’d only share anything without your consent if someone was at serious risk of harm.”

“Reporting to the police is your choice, now or later. The sexual assault centre can see you without the police, and there’s an anonymous scheme where sex workers can warn each other about dangerous clients.”

f.learning: Sex workers face high rates of violence and barriers to care; a non-judgemental, trauma-informed approach is essential. Non-consensual condom removal can constitute rape in English law (consent conditional on condom use). Clarify timing and cycle: emergency contraception — the copper IUD is the most effective method and can be fitted up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse (or up to 5 days after the earliest likely ovulation); oral ulipristal 30 mg (up to 120 hours) is more effective than levonorgestrel around ovulation; give oral EC when an IUD cannot be fitted immediately; wait 5 days after ulipristal before starting hormonal contraception. HIV PEP must start within 72 hours (ideally within 24): refer the same day to a sexual health clinic or SARC for risk assessment, hepatitis B vaccination (accelerated course), STI testing (repeat at window periods: chlamydia and gonorrhoea at 2 weeks, HIV at 45 days, syphilis at 12 weeks). Offer SARC forensic examination and support (self-referral, no police required), explain police reporting is her choice, and mention anonymous reporting schemes (National Ugly Mums). Screen injuries (head, strangulation), safety, coercion, mood and alcohol. Confidentiality: GMC duties apply; no disclosure to her university; information is shared without consent only where there is a serious risk of harm to others or required by law.

knowledge.guideline: FSRH (now CoSRH) Clinical guideline: Emergency contraception (2017, with later amendments) · BHIVA/BASHH UK guideline for the use of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (2021) · GMC Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information (2017) · NHS England Sexual Assault Referral Centres service specification (current) · BASHH UK national guideline on the management of adult and adolescent complainants of sexual assault (current)
knowledge.summary: Non-judgemental, time-critical care: EC (IUD best; ulipristal today), same-day PEP and STI assessment, SARC offered, police her choice, injuries and safety screened, and confidentiality made clear.

points.t: Cu-IUD: most effective; up to 5 days after UPSI or within 5 days of the earliest estimated ovulation. Ulipristal 30 mg: up to 120 hours, more effective than levonorgestrel close to ovulation; reduced by enzyme inducers; wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg (3 mg if BMI over 26 or weight over 70 kg, or with enzyme inducers): up to 72 hours.

Start as soon as possible and within 72 hours. Decisions depend on the source’s likely status and the type of exposure; for receptive vaginal sex with a source of unknown status from a low-prevalence group, PEP is often not recommended, but assault and injury change the assessment — this is for the clinic to decide quickly.
Baseline tests now; repeat chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT at 2 weeks, HIV at 45 days (4th-generation test), syphilis at 12 weeks. Hepatitis B accelerated vaccination if not immune.

SARCs offer forensic examination (vaginal assault: evidence may be recoverable up to 7 days), emergency contraception, PEP, Independent Sexual Violence Advisers and counselling; self-referral without police is possible and samples can be stored.

Ask about strangulation (non-fatal strangulation needs urgent assessment), head injury, ongoing threats, coercion or exploitation; anonymous reporting (National Ugly Mums); support organisations for sex workers.
Record clinically relevant facts accurately but proportionately; patients can discuss record wording and sensitive-information settings. Universities have no right to GP records without consent.
Pass: correct EC and PEP referral. Clear pass: done without judgement, with the assault named, injuries and safety screened, and the university fear answered so she engages.

model.text: Hi Mia, I’m Dr Clarke. Thanks for your message. Are you somewhere private where you can talk?
Yes, I’m at home. I need the morning-after pill — I know it’s late — and an STI test. Something happened at work.
Of course. Can you tell me as much as you’re comfortable with about what happened, and when?
Saturday night, about eleven. I’m an escort. He took the condom off halfway. When I told him to stop, he slapped me and grabbed my arm.
I’m really sorry that happened. It wasn’t your fault. Are you hurt? Any head injury, blacking out, or did he put pressure on your neck?
Bruise on my arm, sore cheek. Nothing on my neck. No blacking out.
When did your last period start, and are you using any contraception or taking any medicines?
Thirteen days ago, regular. Just condoms. No medicines.
Do you know anything about his HIV status? And are you safe — does anyone else control your work or money?
No idea about HIV. I work for myself. I’m scared to go back to the flat, though.

Taking off a condom without your agreement can be rape, and hitting you is assault. There are two clocks running: HIV prevention medicine has to start within 72 hours — so about a day and a half left — and the coil, the best emergency contraception, can go in up to five days.
model.why: Names the offence; explains time-critical options

model.text: Will this go on my record? I’m a student nurse. If uni finds out, I’m finished.

What you tell me stays within your healthcare. I won’t tell your university, and they can’t see your records without your consent. I’d only share anything without permission if someone was at serious risk. We can talk about how it’s worded in your notes.

I’ll prescribe ulipristal now so you’re covered, and ring the sexual health clinic to see you today for the coil, the HIV medicine assessment, hepatitis B vaccine and tests. If you take ulipristal, wait five days before starting any pill.
Do I have to go to the police?

That’s your choice, now or later. The sexual assault centre can examine you and keep evidence without involving the police, and they have advisers who can support you. There’s also National Ugly Mums, where you can report him anonymously to warn others.
How are you sleeping and coping? Any thoughts of harming yourself?
Shaky, not sleeping. No thoughts like that. A bit more wine.

Let’s recap: ulipristal from the pharmacy now, the clinic this afternoon, think about the SARC, and I’ll call you on Friday. If you get headaches, vomiting or feel unsafe, call 999. What will you do first?
Pharmacy, then the clinic today. I’ll think about the SARC. Thank you for not being weird about it.

social.t: Sex workers experience high levels of violence and often avoid services for fear of judgement or police involvement.
Student or professional status raises fear of exposure; reassurance about confidentiality increases engagement.

legal.t: Consent conditional on condom use: deliberate removal without agreement can be rape (Sexual Offences Act 2003; case law).
Selling sex is not illegal in England; some related activities are. Avoid offering legal opinions beyond safety advice; signpost specialist support.

professional.t: GMC: disclose without consent only where required by law or justified in the public interest (serious harm). Universities have no access to records without consent.

community.t: Sexual health clinic; SARC and ISVA; National Ugly Mums; specialist sex worker support projects; Rape Crisis.

playbook.diagnosis: Unprotected intercourse through non-consensual condom removal with physical assault ~40 hours ago, mid-cycle — needs EC, PEP assessment, STI and hepatitis B care, and assault support.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “What happened was an assault. Medically, we need to prevent pregnancy, consider HIV prevention, and test for infections — and some of that has a time limit.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted this sorted quietly — we can do that, and your university won’t be told.”
management.psychosocial: Safety for return to work; anonymous reporting; mood follow-up.
sharedPlan: Same-day sexual health clinic: Cu-IUD, PEP assessment, hepatitis B, STI tests
safetyNet: 999 if in danger or new head injury symptoms
Contact the practice if low mood worsens

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by judgement, by missing the time limits, or by treating an assault as a contraception request.

items.fail: Moralising or visibly awkward reaction to her work.
items.why: She stops disclosing and may disengage from care.
items.fix: Neutral, curious and calm; focus on her health and safety.

items.fail: Gives levonorgestrel and a routine STI test in two weeks.
items.why: Misses the more effective options (IUD, ulipristal) and the 72-hour PEP window.
items.fix: IUD first-line, ulipristal today, same-day clinic for PEP assessment.

items.fail: Never asks about injuries or safety.
items.why: Head injury, strangulation and ongoing risk need assessment.
items.fix: Ask directly about head, neck and safety.

wordPics.clearFail: Judgemental; prescribes levonorgestrel and books routine tests; does not ask about the incident, injuries or PEP.
wordPics.fail: Correct EC but no PEP urgency or SARC offer; confidentiality fear not addressed so she disengages.
wordPics.pass: Non-judgemental; correct EC with IUD offered; same-day clinic for PEP and tests; SARC and police options; injury and safety screen.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus names the assault clearly, answers the university fear precisely, mentions anonymous reporting, screens mood and alcohol, and agrees a specific follow-up.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.

Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
